items.stem: Which statement correctly explains the meaning of 'absolute liability'?
options: A new and intervening act, such as an unforeseeable act of a third party or of the victim, that breaks the chain of causation.
The mental element of a crime, such as intention or recklessness, that the prosecution must prove the defendant had at the time of the actus reus.
A minor offence, often of strict liability, concerned with matters of social concern such as food safety, pollution or sale of alcohol, rather than "truly criminal" behaviour.
An offence where no mens rea is required at all and the actus reus need not even be voluntary, such as R v Larsonneur (1933).
items.answer: An offence where no mens rea is required at all and the actus reus need not even be voluntary, such as R v Larsonneur (1933).
items.markingKey: absolute liability: An offence where no mens rea is required at all and the actus reus need not even be voluntary, such as R v Larsonneur (1933).

items.stem: Which statement correctly explains the meaning of 'Judicial Appointments Commission'?

Protection for senior judges, who hold office during good behaviour and can be removed only by the monarch following an address by both Houses of Parliament.
Checking potential jurors' backgrounds, either routine police checks for criminal records or, exceptionally, wider checks in national security cases.
items.answer: The independent body created by the Constitutional Reform Act 2005 to select candidates for judicial office in England and Wales solely on merit.
items.markingKey: Judicial Appointments Commission: The independent body created by the Constitutional Reform Act 2005 to select candidates for judicial office in England and Wales solely on merit.

items.stem: Explain why gross negligence manslaughter has been criticised as circular.
items.answer: The jury is asked whether the negligence was so bad as to be criminal, so in effect it decides that conduct is criminal because it is criminal; this leaves the definition vague and outcomes inconsistent.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: circular test explained; 1 mark: consequence – uncertainty/inconsistency. [3]

items.stem: Explain why distinguishing is sometimes criticised.
items.answer: Judges may draw very fine or artificial distinctions to avoid a precedent, which makes the law complex and uncertain and difficult to predict.

items.stem: Diego threw a glass bottle at Ana in a bus station in Istanbul, but missed and hit Arjun, who was cut on the face. Discuss Diego's liability, applying the doctrine of transferred malice. Explain the relevant law, apply it to the facts and evaluate the strength of any arguments available.
items.answer: Law: transferred malice: mens rea against one victim transfers to the actual victim of the same type of offence (R v Latimer); it does not transfer between different types of offence (R v Pembliton); no "double transfer" (Attorney-General's Reference (No 3 of 1994)). Application: Diego had mens rea towards Ana; the mens rea is transferred to Arjun, because the offence is the same type (offence against the person). Conclusion: Diego can be liable for the injury to Arjun.
items.markingKey: AO1 Knowledge [5]: identifies transferred malice; accurate statement of the law, e.g. transferred malice: mens rea against one victim transfers to the actual victim of the same type of offence (R v Latimer); it does not transfer between different types of offence (R v Pembliton); no "double transfer" (Attorney-General's Reference (No 3 of 1994)). AO2 Application [6]: applies the rules to the facts, e.g. Diego had mens rea towards Ana; the mens rea is transferred to Arjun, because the offence is the same type (offence against the person). Conclusion [1]: Diego can be liable for the injury to Arjun Top band needs case authority used accurately and every relevant issue applied, not just described. [12]

items.stem: Ethan, aged 45, has received a summons for jury service at Doha Crown Court. Ethan is currently on bail for a theft charge. Advise Ethan whether Ethan can or must serve on the jury. Apply the relevant legal rules and case law to the facts, considering any alternative arguments.
items.answer: Law: Juries Act 1974: aged 18-75, on the electoral register and resident in the UK for at least five years since age 13; disqualified: those on bail, those with certain sentences (five years or more for life; any custody or community order in the last ten years) and mentally disordered persons; excusal and deferral are discretionary; police officers and lawyers are eligible since the CJA 2003. Application: Ethan is 45; jurors must be 18-75; Ethan is currently on bail for a theft charge, so Ethan is disqualified while on bail. Conclusion: If within the age range, Ethan is disqualified while on bail; anyone outside 18-75 cannot serve.

items.stem: Diego drank several cans of strong beer and some wine at a party in Dubai. Diego then punched Felix, causing a black eye. Discuss whether Diego's intoxication provides a defence. Explain the relevant legal rules before applying them.
items.answer: Law: voluntary intoxication: a defence to specific intent offences only if D did not form the intent (Sheehan and Moore); no defence to basic intent offences (Majewski); Dutch courage is no defence (Gallagher); involuntary intoxication: a defence only if D lacked mens rea; a drunken intent is still an intent (Kingston). Application: the intoxication was voluntary; the offence is s47 ABH, a basic intent offence; voluntary intoxication is no defence (Majewski). Conclusion: The effect of the voluntary intoxication depends on whether the offence is of specific or basic intent: voluntary intoxication is no defence (Majewski).

items.stem: A national emergency caused by severe flooding has hit the country. Parliament is not sitting and urgent rules are needed to ration fuel supplies. Arjun, a government lawyer, is asked how this can be done. Advise Arjun on the most suitable form of law-making and any safeguards. In your answer, refer to decided cases and assess how a court is likely to decide.
items.answer: Law: Orders in Council are made by the King and Privy Council; the Civil Contingencies Act 2004 allows emergency regulations when there is not time to pass an Act; emergency regulations must be laid before Parliament and lapse after 30 days unless approved. Application: the emergency caused by severe flooding creates an urgent need that the slow Bill procedure cannot meet; safeguards ensure Parliament can still scrutinise the regulations. Conclusion: An Order in Council under the Civil Contingencies Act 2004 is the appropriate method, subject to later parliamentary approval.
items.markingKey: AO1 Knowledge [3]: identifies Orders in Council in an emergency under the Civil Contingencies Act 2004; accurate statement of the law, e.g. Orders in Council are made by the King and Privy Council; the Civil Contingencies Act 2004 allows emergency regulations when there is not time to pass an Act; emergency regulations must be laid before Parliament and lapse after 30 days unless approved. items.stem: Which of the following best defines 'distinguishing'?

A method of avoiding a precedent by showing that the material facts of the present case are sufficiently different from those of the earlier case, so the earlier ratio does not apply.
The advantage of precedent that lawyers and the public can predict how the law will be applied because courts follow earlier decisions.
Where a court expresses the opinion that an earlier decision was wrong but does not overrule it because it is not necessary to decide the point.
items.answer: A method of avoiding a precedent by showing that the material facts of the present case are sufficiently different from those of the earlier case, so the earlier ratio does not apply.

items.stem: Explain why the mischief rule is said to promote justice.
items.answer: It allows judges to look at why the Act was passed and to give effect to Parliament's intention to remedy a problem, so the law is applied sensibly and loopholes are closed, as in Smith v Hughes.

items.stem: Using your knowledge of the law, evaluate the effectiveness of the criminal appeal system in correcting miscarriages of justice.
items.answer: For: two routes from the magistrates' court; Court of Appeal can quash unsafe convictions; CCRC investigates miscarriages and has referred many cases; double jeopardy reform allows guilty people to be retried (R v Dobson). Against: leave is required and many appeals fail; the Court of Appeal is reluctant to interfere with jury verdicts; the CCRC has limited resources and long delays; the "real possibility" test is restrictive. Conclusion: The system corrects many errors but delays and restrictive tests mean some miscarriages remain.

items.stem: In Patel v Northgate Ltd (fictional, 2021), the Supreme Court held that a landlord was liable for damp caused by a broken gutter. The judge added that "the same principle would probably apply to a free public sports facility". Ana is now bringing a similar case in the High Court. Explain which parts of the earlier judgment the High Court must follow in Ana's case. Your answer should explain the relevant law, refer to decided cases and reach a reasoned conclusion.
items.answer: Law: the ratio decidendi of a higher court binds lower courts through stare decisis; obiter dicta are persuasive only (R v Howe and R v Gotts); the material facts must be sufficiently similar for the ratio to apply. Application: the Supreme Court is above the High Court in the hierarchy; the holding that a landlord was liable for damp caused by a broken gutter is the ratio and binds the High Court if the material facts are similar; the remark that "the same principle would probably apply to a free public sports facility" is obiter and need not be followed. Conclusion: The High Court is bound by the ratio if the facts are similar but may choose whether to follow the obiter comment.
items.markingKey: AO1 Knowledge [5]: identifies the distinction between the binding ratio decidendi and persuasive obiter dicta; accurate statement of the law, e.g. the ratio decidendi of a higher court binds lower courts through stare decisis; obiter dicta are persuasive only (R v Howe and R v Gotts); the material facts must be sufficiently similar for the ratio to apply. items.stem: Section 1 of the (fictional) Alcohol (Young Persons) Act 2017 provides that "it is an offence to sell alcohol to a person under 18 in a shop". Nadia sold beer to a 16-year-old through a website that delivered to the buyer's home. Explain how a court using the purposive approach would interpret the section, and advise Nadia. Refer to at least one decided case.
items.answer: Law: literal rule: words are given their plain, ordinary meaning even if the result is absurd (Whiteley v Chappell, LNER v Berriman); purposive approach: the court looks for the purpose of Parliament and interprets the words to achieve it (Jones v Tower Boot; R (Quintavalle) v Secretary of State for Health); the court may use extrinsic aids such as Hansard (Pepper v Hart) and explanatory notes to identify the purpose. Application: literal rule: Nadia would be not guilty, since the sale did not take place in a shop; purposive approach: the purpose was to prevent young people obtaining alcohol from retailers; Nadia would be guilty because online sales give under-18s the same access to alcohol that the Act aimed to stop. Conclusion: The outcome depends on the approach taken; a modern court looking at the purpose of the Act would probably find Nadia guilty.

items.stem: Jonas chased with a knife Mohammed in a car park in Doha. To escape, Mohammed stopped to take selfies and then deliberately lay down in the road and was seriously injured. (a) Identify the main legal issue raised by these facts. (b) Discuss whether Jonas is the legal cause of Mohammed's injuries.
items.answer: (a) Whether the victim's own act breaks the chain of causation. (b) Law: factual causation: "but for" test; the victim's reaction does not break the chain if it is reasonably foreseeable (R v Roberts); only a "daft" reaction, out of proportion to the threat, breaks the chain (R v Williams 1992); the free, deliberate and informed act of the victim may break the chain (R v Kennedy (No 2)). Application: but for Jonas's conduct, Mohammed would not have been injured; Mohammed stopped to take selfies and then deliberately lay down in the road, which is a "daft" and unforeseeable reaction that may break the chain (R v Williams). Conclusion: Jonas is probably not liable for the injuries.

items.stem: Explain the difference between recklessness and negligence.
items.answer: Recklessness is subjective: the defendant foresees a risk and unjustifiably takes it; negligence is objective: the defendant falls below the standard of the reasonable person, whether or not they foresaw the risk.

items.stem: Felix has been diagnosed with paranoid schizophrenia. During an argument in a car park in Jakarta, Felix attacked and killed Daniel. Felix had not taken any alcohol or drugs. (a) Identify the main legal issue raised by these facts. (b) Outline the law that applies, with supporting authority. (c) Discuss whether Felix can rely on the defence of diminished responsibility.
items.answer: (a) The partial defence of diminished responsibility. (b) s2 Homicide Act 1957 (as amended by s52 CJA 2009): abnormality of mental functioning from a recognised medical condition; it must substantially impair D's ability to understand his conduct, form a rational judgement or exercise self-control (R v Golds: important or weighty); it must provide an explanation for the killing; D must prove it on the balance of probabilities; intoxication does not prevent the defence (R v Dietschmann). (c) Law: s2 Homicide Act 1957 (as amended by s52 CJA 2009): abnormality of mental functioning from a recognised medical condition; it must substantially impair D's ability to understand his conduct, form a rational judgement or exercise self-control (R v Golds: important or weighty); it must provide an explanation for the killing; D must prove it on the balance of probabilities; intoxication does not prevent the defence (R v Dietschmann). Application: paranoid schizophrenia is a recognised medical condition; medical evidence must show it substantially impaired Felix's abilities; Felix had not taken any alcohol or drugs; under Dietschmann the jury asks whether the condition itself substantially impaired Felix. Conclusion: Felix has a good argument for diminished responsibility, which would reduce murder to voluntary manslaughter if proved on the balance of probabilities.

items.stem: A Bill on banning trail hunting with dogs has been passed by the House of Commons, but the House of Lords voted it down two months ago. The Bill is not a money Bill. Amara, a government minister, asks whether it can still become law. Advise Amara whether the Bill can become law without the agreement of the House of Lords. Apply the relevant legal rules and case law to the facts, considering any alternative arguments.
items.answer: Law: under the Parliament Acts 1911 and 1949 the Lords can delay a non-money Bill for about one year; the Bill must be passed by the Commons in two successive sessions, then it can receive Royal Assent without the Lords' consent; R (Jackson) v Attorney-General (2005) confirmed that Acts passed in this way are valid; by the Salisbury convention the Lords do not usually oppose manifesto Bills at second reading. Application: the Bill on banning trail hunting with dogs is not a money Bill, so the one-year delay applies; the Commons should pass it again in the next session; after that it can be presented for Royal Assent without the Lords. Conclusion: The Bill can become law without the Lords' consent by using the Parliament Acts procedure, after a delay of about one year.

items.stem: Mohammed shouted violent threats at Sipho in a car park in Mexico City. To escape, Sipho stopped to take selfies and then deliberately lay down in the road and was seriously injured. Discuss whether Mohammed is the legal cause of Sipho's injuries.
items.answer: Law: factual causation: "but for" test; the victim's reaction does not break the chain if it is reasonably foreseeable (R v Roberts); only a "daft" reaction, out of proportion to the threat, breaks the chain (R v Williams 1992); the free, deliberate and informed act of the victim may break the chain (R v Kennedy (No 2)). Application: but for Mohammed's conduct, Sipho would not have been injured; Sipho stopped to take selfies and then deliberately lay down in the road, which is a "daft" and unforeseeable reaction that may break the chain (R v Williams). Conclusion: Mohammed is probably not liable for the injuries.

items.stem: In Okafor v Riverside Council (fictional, 2018), the Supreme Court held that a landlord was liable for damp caused by a broken gutter. The judge added that "the position might be different if the tenant had caused the damage". Noah is now bringing a similar case in the High Court. Explain which parts of the earlier judgment the High Court must follow in Noah's case. Explain the relevant law, apply it to the facts and evaluate the strength of any arguments available.
items.answer: Law: the ratio decidendi of a higher court binds lower courts through stare decisis; obiter dicta are persuasive only (R v Howe and R v Gotts); the material facts must be sufficiently similar for the ratio to apply. Application: the Supreme Court is above the High Court in the hierarchy; the holding that a landlord was liable for damp caused by a broken gutter is the ratio and binds the High Court if the material facts are similar; the remark that "the position might be different if the tenant had caused the damage" is obiter and need not be followed. Conclusion: The High Court is bound by the ratio if the facts are similar but may choose whether to follow the obiter comment.

items.stem: Omar, aged 19, set off fireworks next to a wooden fence in Istanbul. A window was smashed and a passenger was cut. Discuss whether Omar was reckless. Consider all the relevant issues and reach a justified conclusion.
items.answer: Law: recklessness is subjective: the defendant must be aware of a risk which, in the circumstances known to him, it is unreasonable to take (R v G 2003); R v Cunningham (1957) also requires foresight of the risk; MPC v Caldwell objective test no longer applies. items.stem: Section 1 of the (fictional) Public Parks (Safety) Act 2014 provides that "it is an offence to bring a vehicle into a public park". Freya drove an ambulance into the park to reach an injured jogger. Apply the literal rule, the golden rule and the mischief rule to advise whether Freya has committed the offence. Apply the relevant legal rules and case law to the facts, considering any alternative arguments.
items.answer: Law: literal rule: words are given their plain, ordinary meaning even if the result is absurd (Whiteley v Chappell, LNER v Berriman); golden rule: the literal meaning may be modified to avoid an absurd result (R v Allen, narrow approach) or a repugnant one (Re Sigsworth, wide approach); mischief rule: the court asks what problem the Act was passed to remedy (Heydon's Case; Smith v Hughes). Application: literal rule: Freya would be guilty, since an ambulance is a vehicle; golden rule: Freya would be not guilty, since it would be absurd and repugnant to convict emergency services for saving life; mischief rule: the mischief was the danger and disturbance caused to park users by motor traffic; Freya would be not guilty because the Act was not aimed at emergency vehicles helping park users. Conclusion: The outcome depends on the approach taken; a modern court looking at the purpose of the Act would probably find Freya not guilty.

items.stem: Yusuf threw a brick through the window of a house occupied by Aisha outside a shop in Lima. Aisha, who was a healthy 25-year-old, fell and hit their head on the pavement and died. Discuss whether Yusuf is guilty of unlawful act manslaughter.
items.answer: Law: there must be an unlawful act that is a crime (R v Lamb; R v Franklin); the act must be dangerous: sober and reasonable people would recognise the risk of some harm (R v Church; DPP v Newbury and Jones); the reasonable person knows what D knew or would have seen (R v Dawson; R v Watson); the act must cause the death, and D need not foresee harm. Application: Yusuf's act was a criminal damage, a criminal act; Aisha's condition was irrelevant to dangerousness; the jury must decide whether a sober and reasonable person would recognise a risk of some harm from the act; causation: Aisha's death followed the act; the thin skull rule applies. Conclusion: Yusuf is likely to be guilty of unlawful act manslaughter if the act was dangerous in the Church sense; the victim's condition being irrelevant to dangerousness affects this.

items.stem: Explain why duress is not a defence to murder.
items.answer: The House of Lords in R v Howe held that the law should not allow a person to take an innocent life to save their own; ordinary people are expected to be heroic in such cases, and allowing the defence could help terrorists and gangs.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: sanctity of innocent life; 1 mark: policy/risk of abuse. [2]

items.stem: Describe the training required to qualify as a solicitor.
items.answer: A degree (in any subject) or equivalent; passing SQE1 (legal knowledge) and SQE2 (practical skills); two years of qualifying work experience; and satisfying the SRA's character and suitability requirements.
items.markingKey: 1 mark degree; 1 mark SQE1 and SQE2; 1 mark qualifying work experience; 1 mark character and suitability. [4]

items.stem: With reference to decided cases and statutory provisions where relevant, "The doctrine of precedent achieves a good balance between certainty and flexibility." Discuss.
items.answer: For: certainty from stare decisis and the hierarchy; flexibility from distinguishing, the Practice Statement and Young exceptions. Against: Practice Statement used rarely; Court of Appeal tightly bound (Davis v Johnson); distinguishing can produce artificial distinctions. Conclusion: The balance generally favours certainty, with flexibility available but used sparingly.

items.stem: Section 1 of the (fictional) Public Parks (Safety) Act 2014 provides that "it is an offence to bring a vehicle into a public park". Daniel rode a child's push scooter along a park path. Explain how a court using the purposive approach would interpret the section, and advise Daniel. Your answer should explain the relevant law, refer to decided cases and reach a reasoned conclusion.
items.answer: Law: literal rule: words are given their plain, ordinary meaning even if the result is absurd (Whiteley v Chappell, LNER v Berriman); purposive approach: the court looks for the purpose of Parliament and interprets the words to achieve it (Jones v Tower Boot; R (Quintavalle) v Secretary of State for Health); the court may use extrinsic aids such as Hansard (Pepper v Hart) and explanatory notes to identify the purpose. Application: literal rule: Daniel would be guilty, since a scooter is literally a vehicle; purposive approach: the purpose was to prevent the danger and disturbance caused to park users by motor traffic; Daniel would be not guilty because a toy scooter does not create the danger the Act was aimed at. Conclusion: The outcome depends on the approach taken; a modern court looking at the purpose of the Act would probably find Daniel not guilty.

items.stem: Amara stabbed Tomás during an argument in Toronto. Tomás was taken to hospital, where Tomás was declared brain-dead and the life-support machine was switched off. Tomás died. Discuss whether Amara caused Tomás's death. Explain the relevant legal rules before applying them.
items.answer: Law: factual causation: but for the defendant's act the result would not have occurred (R v White); legal causation: the act must be an operating and substantial cause (R v Smith); medical treatment breaks the chain only if so independent and potent (R v Cheshire), e.g. palpably wrong (R v Jordan); the thin skull rule applies (R v Blaue). Application: but for the stabbing Tomás would not have been in hospital, so factual causation is satisfied; here Tomás was declared brain-dead and the life-support machine was switched off, which raises switching off life support does not break the chain (R v Malcherek); so Amara is liable for the death. Conclusion: Amara is liable for the death.

items.stem: Grace is a nurse caring for Jonas on a hospital ward. Grace made a single minor error that an experienced colleague might also have made. As a result, Jonas died. Discuss whether Grace is guilty of gross negligence manslaughter. In your answer, refer to decided cases and assess how a court is likely to decide.
items.answer: Law: R v Adomako (1994): duty of care, breach, causing death, and negligence so gross it should be criminal; there must be an obvious and serious risk of death (Misra and Srivastava), foreseeable at the time of breach (R v Rose); a duty can exist even in an illegal enterprise (R v Wacker). Application: Grace owed Jonas a duty as a nurse caring for Jonas on a hospital ward (doctor/nurse-patient relationship (Adomako)); Grace made a single minor error that an experienced colleague might also have made, which is a breach; the negligence is probably not gross, so the jury will decide whether it was so bad as to be criminal. Conclusion: Grace owed and breached a duty; liability depends on the jury finding the negligence gross: here it is probably not gross.
